lines.text: Imagine you're stocking a giant industrial freezer... when the door slams shut behind you.
It's minus twenty degrees Celsius, and fans keep pushing freezing air across your body.
You push the door. It won't budge.
Within seconds, you feel cold. But that's just nerves in your skin sounding the alarm. Your core is still normal: around thirty-seven degrees.
To protect it, your body squeezes the blood vessels in your skin, cutting the flow of warm blood to your hands.
Then the shivering starts: rapid, involuntary muscle contractions that burn energy for heat.
But heat is escaping everywhere: into the air and walls, out with every breath, and into anything you touch.
Your fingers go numb and clumsy. And the metal-clad walls can block your signal.
Then you remember: most walk-in freezers have an emergency release inside the door.
But this one is jammed with ice.
You hurry to break it free... and the frosted floor takes your legs out.
Hours can pass. Your core slowly cools, and below thirty-five degrees, you have hypothermia.
In this mild stage, you'll likely shiver violently. Your hands fumble, your speech may slur, and your judgment starts to slip.
While you wait for help: get off the metal floor, which drains heat from you. Sit on cardboard, tuck your hands into your armpits, and curl up.
Somewhere below thirty-two, something frightening can happen: the shivering fades, then stops. Not because you're warm, but because your body is running out of ways to fight.
Confusion and drowsiness creep in. You might not even realize you're in danger.
Below about twenty-eight, people usually lose consciousness, and the heart's rhythm can turn dangerously unstable.
So... could you survive?
In cold air, serious hypothermia usually takes hours, not minutes. But there's no fixed countdown.
It depends on the temperature, moving air, your clothing, staying dry, your body and health... and how fast you're found.
Feeling cold is your body's alarm. The danger deepens when that alarm goes quiet.
In rare cases, doctors have revived people from astonishingly low body temperatures. That's why rescuers say: nobody's dead until they're warm and dead.
